identification.summary: Elderwood is the name Symantec gave in September 2012 to a systematic espionage group that reused components of an infrastructure it called the 'Elderwood platform' and that Symantec tracked back to the 2009 Operation Aurora attacks on Google and other companies [S1][S2]. Symantec reported the group had exploited at least eight zero-day vulnerabilities since late 2010, all in Internet Explorer or Adobe Flash Player, and that it was moving from spear-phishing toward watering-hole attacks against defense supply chain targets [S2][S6]. Symantec tied a December 2012 Internet Explorer zero-day (CVE-2012-4792) served from the Council on Foreign Relations website to the same group [S6][S7]. MITRE ATT&CK tracks it as G0066, a suspected Chinese cyber espionage group reportedly responsible for Operation Aurora [S8].
identification.firstObserved: 2009: Symantec tracks the group back to the 2009 Operation Aurora attacks [S2].
identification.notes: Symantec says the name comes from a source-code variable used by the attackers [S2]. Malpedia lists Elderwood, Elderwood Gang, G0066, SIG22 and SNEAKY PANDA; MITRE lists Elderwood Gang, Beijing Group and Sneaky Panda [S8]. No Microsoft Typhoon/Storm name was found for this cluster in the sources gathered. Symantec separately named 'Hidden Lynx' in 2013 and linked it to Aurora through shared malware; CrowdStrike tracked that group as 'Aurora Panda'. These are distinct vendor clusters from Elderwood/Sneaky Panda and should not be merged without primary evidence [S9].

attribution.sponsor: Suspected People's Republic of China. Google stated the Aurora attacks originated in China [S2]; MITRE describes Elderwood as a suspected Chinese cyber espionage group [S8].
attribution.confidence: Symantec's 2012 report did not name China or a geographic origin and said only that the group's sophistication probably indicated support from organized crime or a nation state [S2]. MITRE's characterization is 'suspected' [S8]. No US government attribution of the Elderwood cluster by name was found in the sources gathered; 2013 press reporting citing unnamed US officials described the Google breach as by Chinese hackers [S5].
attribution.basis: Symantec analysis of shared infrastructure, packer license and code artifacts (for example a misspelled 'HeapSpary' function) linking successive zero-day campaigns [S2][S6]; MITRE ATT&CK group entry [S8].

objectives: Strategic espionage. Google initially pointed to Gmail accounts of Chinese human rights activists and intellectual property [S5]; US officials later told the Washington Post the Google intrusion reached a database of law-enforcement and FISA surveillance orders, apparently to identify Chinese intelligence operatives under US surveillance [S5]. Symantec reported that the group's primary targets were usually members of the defense supply chain [S2].

sectors: Defense industrial base and defense supply chain manufacturers [S2]
Think tanks / foreign policy organizations (Council on Foreign Relations website) [S6][S7]
regions: United States (Council on Foreign Relations watering hole) [S7]

capabilities.summary: Repeated use of zero-day exploits in Internet Explorer and Adobe Flash Player, at least eight from 2010 to fall 2012 and a ninth (CVE-2012-4792) in December 2012 [S2][S6]. Aurora used an Internet Explorer zero-day (CVE-2010-0249) delivered via spear-phishing links in email and instant messages to drop the Hydraq remote access trojan [S1][S2]. From 2012 the group increasingly used watering-hole (strategic web compromise) attacks, [S2][S7]. Symantec described shared tooling ('Elderwood platform'), a common commercial packer license, and reuse of exploit components across campaigns [S2][S6]. MITRE lists associated software including PoisonIvy, Hydraq, Briba, Naid, Wiarp, Vasport, Pasam, Nerex and Linfo [S8].

campaigns.name: Operation Aurora
campaigns.summary: Intrusions against Google and other companies using the IE zero-day CVE-2010-0249 to install a remote access trojan, described by McAfee in January 2010; Symantec later tied the Elderwood group to these attacks.

campaigns.name: Aurora surveillance-database disclosure
campaigns.summary: Washington Post reporting, citing unnamed US officials, said the Google intruders accessed a database of surveillance orders including FISA orders.

campaigns.name: Elderwood zero-day series
campaigns.summary: Symantec counted at least eight zero-days in IE and Flash Player exploited since late 2010, four in about 16 weeks in spring and summer 2012, mainly against defense supply chain targets.

campaigns.name: CVE-2012-1889 watering hole
campaigns.summary: Symantec linked a June 2012 site serving CVE-2012-1889 with a movie.swf file to the Elderwood Project.

campaigns.name: Symantec 'The Elderwood Project' report
campaigns.summary: Symantec published its report describing the Elderwood platform, the shift to watering-hole attacks, and the defense supply chain focus.

campaigns.name: Council on Foreign Relations watering hole (CVE-2012-4792)
campaigns.summary: The CFR website was compromised to serve an IE 6-8 zero-day; Symantec assessed it as a continuation of the Elderwood Project; Microsoft later issued out-of-band fix MS13-008.

diamond.adversary: Suspected PRC espionage group (Symantec: likely nation-state or organized-crime backed; MITRE: suspected Chinese) [S2][S8].
diamond.capability: Serial IE and Flash zero-days, Hydraq and related backdoors, commercial packer, shared 'Elderwood platform' exploit components [S1][S2][S6][S8].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised legitimate websites used as watering holes (e.g., CFR), spear-phishing links via email and instant message [S1][S7].
diamond.victim: Defense supply chain manufacturers, technology and internet firms (Google), human rights activists and NGOs, think tanks [S2][S5][S7][S8].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection on PRC dissidents, US technology and defense IP, and US counterintelligence activity (surveillance orders) [S5].
diamond.technology: Unpatched Internet Explorer 6-8 and Adobe Flash Player on Windows endpoints; trust in frequently visited policy and industry websites [S1][S6][S7].

gaps: Original Symantec 'The Elderwood Project' PDF and Symantec Connect blog could not be opened; details come from search summaries and press coverage of them [S2][S6].
The Washington Post article was not opened directly; reliance is on secondary coverage [S5].
MITRE ATT&CK G0066 page and CFR Cyber Operations Tracker 'Sneaky Panda' entry could not be fetched; alias and description data are from search-result summaries.
No Microsoft threat actor name identified for Elderwood; Microsoft mapping not checked.
Relationship between Elderwood/Sneaky Panda and Symantec's Hidden Lynx / CrowdStrike's Aurora Panda is unresolved; shared Aurora malware does not establish identity [S9].
No public activity explicitly attributed to Elderwood after early 2013 was found; current status is unknown.
No US government attribution naming Elderwood or a specific PRC organization was found.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain includes user endpoints running browsers and plug-ins, and the third-party websites (policy, industry, supplier) that DoD and DIB personnel routinely visit [S7]. STEP 2: Historic reliance on browser and Flash zero-days means patch status alone does not bound the threat; defense supply chain firms are an indirect path to defense programs [S2][S6]. STEP 3: Doctrinal template is strategic web compromise or spear-phishing link, browser exploit, RAT such as Hydraq, then collection of IP and sensitive databases [S1][S2][S5]. STEP 4: MLCOA is persistent IP theft from DIB suppliers via watering holes. MDCOA is access to counterintelligence or sensitive legal-process data, as reported for the Google surveillance-order database [S5]. Candidate indicators: unexpected script injection on frequently visited partner sites, heap-spray exploit pages targeting legacy browsers, and Hydraq-family beacons [S1][S6].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness should track compromise of external websites frequented by the force, not only DoDIN assets [S7]. (2) Zero-day use means mitigation (browser isolation, plug-in removal) must be pre-authorized rather than waiting on vendor patches [S6]. (3) Mission assurance depends on DIB supplier hygiene; coordinate with DC3 and the DIB CS program when supplier compromise is suspected [S2]. (4) Coordinate with law enforcement and counterintelligence, since the reported Aurora objective included surveillance-order data [S5].
